newsitem.title: HONG KONG: IPO VIEW-Host of China play IPOs seen before HK handover.
newsitem.headline: IPO VIEW-Host of China play IPOs seen before HK handover.

text.p: Hong Kong is set for a rash of initial public offerings (IPO) of China plays in the run-up to the territory's July 1 return to Chinese sovereignty.

More than 10 China plays, including locally based firms, companies affiliated with Chinese authorities, and Chinese enterprises' H-shares, are queueing up for a Hong Kong listing ahead of the territory's handover at midnight on June 30.
Analysts generally expect keen interest in China plays and mainland companies to continue through the handover period, despite fears of further rises in U.S. interest rates.

"Investors are likely to switch to less interest rate-sensitive stocks such as H-shares and red chips as a kind of defensive move and that will aid sentiment towards this kind of IPO," said Tony Yung, head of research of Tai Fook Securities.
H-shares are Hong Kong-listed shares of large China-incorporated enterprises, while red-chips are Hong Kong companies with strong China ties and smaller, quasi state-owned China firms.
With Hong Kong the focus of international attention during and after the handover, analysts said this could boost investor response to the new issues.

"Buying interest is always there," said Patrick Cheng, director at HSBC Investment Bank. "In general, we expect (IPO) market sentiment to remain positive given that the political and economic environments are stable."
A positive macroeconomic backdrop is also likely. Analysts are forecasting falling interest rates and faster economic growth in China in the coming 12 months.

In addition, the local market will be watching to see how the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) and Hong Kong's securities watchdog, the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), resolve the issue of supervision of red chips and related asset injections.
"They can remove uncertainty and provide guidelines for their (red chips') future asset injection plans," Yung said. "It will have a positive impact on their IPOs."
SFC chairman Anthony Neoh met his CSRC counterpart Zhou Daojiong in Beijing last week, and newspapers reported that they had reached consensus on rules governing red-chip listings.

Coming to the market in May is Chaozhou Industrials Holdings Ltd, the eel farming unit of red chip Guangnan (Holdings) Ltd. Beijing Enterprise Ltd, which is backed by the capital's municipal government, and Zhuhai municipal government-controlled Chukong Shipping are also expected to seek listings in May.
Tianjin Industrial Ltd, a retail and industrial firm representing the Tianjin municipal government, should be brought to the market in June.
Shenzhen CATIC Group, the Shenzhen investment arm of the state-owned Aviation Industries of China, is tentatively lined up for a Hong Kong listing in July.
Analysts said interest in red-chip IPOs would remain high due to the trend of parent companies injecting China-based operations once those factories had a steady profit stream.
In the H-share category, toll road operator Ninghu Expressway is expected to offer shares, seeking to raise HK$4.0 billion ($515 million) in a new issue in May.
Zhejiang Hangyong Expressway is expected to raise HK$300-HK$400 million in an IPO in May or June. Fertiliser producer Sichuan Chuandong Group is tipped to follow.

"We believe the (H-share) sector has bottomed out and the downside risk is seen limited because the market has more or less discounted their poor earnings results," said an executive director at a regional asset management company. "Investors are likely to refocus on this sector."
Other H-shares expected to seek a listing soon are Beijing North Star, Jiangxi Copper, and China Southern Airlines.
